newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai cabinet reshuffle seen unlikely to revive economy.
newsitem.headline: Thai cabinet reshuffle seen unlikely to revive economy.

text.p: The impending resignation of Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is unlikely to revive the country's slowing economy anytime soon, economic analysts said on Monday.

Whoever succeeds Banharn will have a tough time restoring business confidence after his ruling coalition was blamed for depressing investor sentiment and triggering a bearish mood on the bourse this year, they said.
Banharn was accused by the opposition of condoning corruption and economic mismanagement which it charged had sparked the Thai economy's slowest projected growth in a decade.
Private economists expect the Thai gross domestic product to expand only 6.2 percent this year against 8.6 in 1995.

The front-runner for Banharn's job, Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, was likely to give his ally Deputy Prime Minister Amnuay Viravan a full mandate to tackle economic problems, economists said,

However, Banharn has not named a successor after his announcement on Saturday that he would quit in seven days, and his main Chart Thai Party, which controls 91 seats in the 391-seat House of Representatives, has not agreed to back Chavalit as premier.

Even if Chavalit wins the premiership, analysts said intense political horse trading among the six ruling coalition partners would impede efforts to form a respectable economic team by including non-elected economists in his cabinet.
"A Chavalit-led government with Amnuay taking charge of the economy could not solve all problems. We need to see first who joins his economic team," said Sa-ngad Sathapatpattana of Baring Research.

Sa-ngad said Chavalit, whose New Aspiration Party was the second largest in Banharn's coalition, would need to accommodate Chart Thai's political interests in return for its future backing of national budgets and major economic policies.

"New economic measures would not be clear cut as long as the prime minister's party is not the biggest in parliament. We are basically looking at the same old team that has run the country," Sa-ngad said.
Unelected Finance Minister Bodi Chunnananda told reporters on Monday that he expected to be replaced in any new cabinet and would not make major policy decisions for the time being.
Analysts said this reflected the economic disarray the government was in.

Most analysts gave poor ratings to Banharn's two finance ministers, Bodi and Surakiart Sathirathai, citing their limited finance expertise and saying they had failed to display full commitments to tackling inflation and current account deficit.

"The pressing issue for the new prime minister is to handle serious economic problems. I don't think the business community would see a fresh economic direction as long as Chavalit still needs to share cabinet seats according to party quotas," said analyst Somyos Chaemchoi of the Thai Farmers Research Centre.
Chainarong Intharameesap, chairman of business consultancy CSN and Associates Ltd, did not expect a Chavalit economic team would be more effective than its predecessor.
"We are trapped in the vicious circle under the quota system. Bringing in a few experts as window dressing is not going to change things," Chainarong said.
